findings.issue_text: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key() passes datetime values to math.floor()/math.ceil(), causing TypeError when building response cursors for nonempty results
value_from_cursor() leaves the cursor value numeric, causing subsequent pages to compare a datetime database column against an integer instead of converting it to a timezone-aware datetime
Negative-offset cursors reach Django queryset slicing with a negative bound, raising ValueError and producing a server error
The optimized paginator still uses BasePaginator's keyset query and OFFSET slicing, so large offsets among rows sharing a timestamp retain the existing high-volume performance cost

goldens.comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both comments identify the same issue: negative slice offsets being used on Django querysets in the cursor paginator. The golden comment mentions it will raise an AssertionError while the candidate says ValueError, but they're both identifying the same fundamental problem - that Django querysets don't support negative slicing and this will cause a server error. The slight difference in exception type doesn't change that they're pointing to the same underlying bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: value_from_cursor() leaves the cursor value numeric, causing subsequent pages to compare a datetime database column against an integer instead of converting it to a timezone-aware datetime

adjudication.rationale: The OptimizedCursorPaginator's value_from_cursor() method at line 841 simply returns cursor.value as-is without any conversion. When used with audit logs ordered by '-datetime', the cursor value would be a timestamp that needs to be converted to a datetime object for proper comparison. Looking at the DateTimePaginator (not shown but referenced), it likely has proper datetime conversion. The new OptimizedCursorPaginator lacks this conversion, which would cause type mismatches when comparing datetime columns against integer cursor values in subsequent pagination queries.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The optimized paginator still uses BasePaginator's keyset query and OFFSET slicing, so large offsets among rows sharing a timestamp retain the existing high-volume performance cost

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that OptimizedCursorPaginator extends BasePaginator and uses the same OFFSET-based slicing pattern (queryset[start_offset:stop]). Looking at the diff, the new paginator still uses 'offset = cursor.offset' and 'results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])' which means for large offsets with duplicate timestamp values, the database still needs to scan through all preceding rows. This is a valid architectural concern about the claimed 'performance optimization' not actually addressing the fundamental OFFSET performance issue for high-volume scenarios.
